headline: Uraguchi is 裏 (ura, “back”) plus 口 (kuchi, “opening, door”), with kuchi voiced to guchi.
Aku, “evil”, is from Middle Chinese 惡.
Masukomi is short for masu komyunikēshon, “mass communication”.
Shō ga nai contracts 仕様がない (shiyō ga nai), literally “there is no way”.
Warau is derived from 割る (waru, “to split, to break”): “to be in the act of cracking up”.
Ijō is literally “deviance from normalcy”.
Chikyū is an orthographic borrowing from Chinese 地球 (Dìqiú), coined by Matteo Ricci.
Shō as a suffix is a clipping of 小学校 (shōgakkō).
Shū, “masses”, is from Middle Chinese 眾.
Mi, “body”, is from Proto-Japonic *muy and cognate with 実 (mi, “seed, fruit, offspring”).
Okazu was originally a court-lady word for 数々 (kazukazu, “numerous; varied”): a varied selection of food at table.
Onoono is a reduplication of 己 (ono, “self”).
Pikapika was written fikafika in a 1595 Latin–Portuguese–Japanese dictionary, a reduplication of the root of 光る (hikaru).
Yokubari is the stem of 欲張る (yokubaru, “to be intensely greedy”) and appears in texts from 1813.
Suwaru is derived from 据わる (suwaru).
Chiru, “to scatter”, appears in the Kojiki, completed 712 CE.
Hōhō is from Middle Chinese 方法.
Yudan is “unclear, with multiple theories”, one drawing on the story of a pot of oil (油鉢) in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
Ōkesutora came through English from Latin orchēstra and Ancient Greek ὀρχήστρα.
Saku, “fence”, is from Middle Chinese 柵.
Nawa, “rope”, derives from the verb 綯う (nau, “to plait or twist together into twine or line”).
Zu, “drawing”, is from Middle Chinese 圖.
Sankaku, a triangle, is 三 (san, “three”) plus 角 (kaku, “angle”).
Hei, “wall”, is a spelling pronunciation derived from Sinitic 屏.
Kamera is from English camera, which comes from Latin camera, “chamber or bedchamber”.
Shimai is first attested in the Man'yōshū of 759, from Middle Chinese 姊妹, literally “older sister + younger sister”.
In shigeki, 激 is a daiyōji replacing 戟.
Anki, “learning by heart”, is a Middle Chinese compound, 暗記.
Omoitsuku is omoi, the stem of 思う (omou, “to think, to imagine”), plus 付く (tsuku).
Tetsu, “iron”, is borrowed from Middle Chinese 鐵 (MC thet); Mandarin reads it tiě.
Hotoke, “Buddha”, most likely comes from Proto-Koreanic *Pwutukye, related to modern Korean 부처 (Bucheo).
